title: To someone suffering now
hookLine: a short note can matter more than it seems

lines: A FEW LINES, KEPT FOR YEARS.
cards: It's been on the fridge through two kitchens: a card held up by a magnet, the corners gone soft. It only says a few lines in a friend's handwriting. Nobody would call it literature.

But the person who kept it can tell you exactly what week it arrived, and what that week was like. Yesterday's letter went backward, to someone who can't read it. Today's goes forward, to someone who can.

teach.h: A LETTER BRINGS A TRACE OF THE FRIEND.
teach.b: First, letters as company. Seneca, whose letter about Lyon came up three days ago, wrote to his friend Lucilius about the letters they traded.
A letter from an absent friend, he says, brings something real of that friend: a trace of the hand, a way of being present across a distance. It isn't the same as a visit. It isn't nothing.
Second, comfort both ways. Paul's letter to the Romans opens with a man who can't be there yet.
"For I long to see you," he writes, and then he says what he hopes for: "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me." Notice the word together.
The writer isn't only handing comfort down from above; he expects some to come back. You don't have to share Paul's faith to recognize the shape.
A note to someone suffering is one person reaching toward another across a distance, and either one may end up comforted. Third, keep it short.
Job's friends showed what happens once the explaining starts. A note to someone suffering doesn't explain, fix, or find the silver lining. It doesn't say everything happens for a reason.
It says: I know. I'm thinking of you. I'm here.
Fourth, the line. You're not alone. On the page it can look plain.

teach.h: THEIR NAME, YOUR NAME, ONE TRUE LINE.
teach.b: In a hard week, from a real person, with their name at the bottom, it can be the thing someone keeps on the fridge.
The note works because it's specific: their name, your name, one true sentence between them.

how: People on different paths send cards, letters or messages to the sick and the grieving; Jewish, Christian and Muslim communities each have customs of visiting and writing to those in mourning.

games.q: a coworker's father has just died. you want to write something. which note matches today's lesson?
o: I'm so sorry. I'm thinking of you. — your name
here are five tips for grieving.
games.why: short, specific, no explaining: their loss, one true line, your name.

practice: Let someone come to mind who is having a hard time right now, not the hardest case, just the one who comes, and hold them in mind for a few breaths.
Then, in your head, version the note: their name, one true sentence, your name, and no advice. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer, too.

wordCard.voice: Consolatio, the Latin name for a letter of comfort, like Seneca's to Lucilius, and the kind you might send today. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: 'consolation, comfort', also the name for a letter written to someone grieving, a form Seneca wrote in.

carryVoice: Your line: you're not alone. A note doesn't need to be clever to be kept. Day seven hundred fifty-six, done.
